chain.g: to injure, do harm to, hurt, damage

ety.text: From Middle English noysaunce, from Anglo-Norman nusaunce, nussance and Old French nuisance, from nuisir (“to harm”), from Latin nocēre. Doublet of nocence and nocency.

ex: The neighbor's dog barking throughout the night is a right nuisance - I'm going to complain.
What a nuisance to have to go now!
senses.zh: 討厭的事；麻煩事；討厭的人

senses.d: A person or thing causing annoyance or inconvenience.
ex: You can be such a nuisance when you don't get your way.
senses.zh: 麻煩事；討厭的事；麻煩人

senses.d: Anything harmful or offensive to the community or to a member of it, for which a legal remedy exists.

grp.label: person or thing causing annoyance or inconvenience

ety.text: Inherited from Old French nuisance, from nuisir (“to harm”) (compare also French nuire), from Latin nocēre; may correspond to Late Latin nocentia.
From Latin incommoditātem; By surface analysis, in- + comodidad.
